title: Sacubitril/valsartan in adults with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction
question: In adults with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction, what is the hazard of a first cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization with sacubitril/valsartan compared with enalapril?
_prose_rule: Every text field is PROSE unless it is on the validator's numeric list. Prose may not restate a number the object holds structurally.
_sourcing_rule: Every measured input carries the verbatim sentence it was read from and a resolvable link to the layer it was read from. Every cell records all five mandated source layers, with a date on every check, so a layer that held nothing is distinguishable from a layer nobody opened. Derived transforms -- the log point and log standard error of each ratio, and the pooled summary -- are computed here and are not claimed to appear in any source.
_estimand_rule: The measure is part of the question, not a presentation choice. This object pools TIME-TO-FIRST-EVENT HAZARD RATIOS for the composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization, and nothing else. A recurrent-event rate ratio, a hierarchical win ratio and a biomarker ratio-of-change are different quantities that answer different questions, and each trial excluded for reporting one is shown with that reason rather than deleted.
single_tier_because: Every cell's PRIMARY source is the open-access primary publication, and the tier tag on each cell names that layer. That is a real uniformity and it is not the absence of a cascade: each cell's `cascade` block records all five mandated layers, and between them the cells carry found records at the FDA, EMA, registry and prior-synthesis layers as well. The reason the primary tier is the same everywhere is stated on the cell that has to argue for it: what these cells STORE is a point estimate together with a two-sided interval, and the primary publication is the only layer that prints both. On the PARADIGM-HF cell -- the ONE cell where the regulator layers hold anything at all -- they confirm the counts, the denominators and the point estimate exactly, and that agreement is recorded on the cell; they are still not the primary tier there, because they report significance against one-sided alphas and taking a point from one layer and an interval from another would manufacture a quantity no source states. On the other two cells the regulator layers hold NOTHING and the cascade records them as not available with a dated reason, so no confirmation is claimed from them and none should be read into this sentence.
completeness_statement: FULL BUILD. Every randomised trial located that compares sacubitril/valsartan with enalapril in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction AND reports the composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization as a time-to-first hazard ratio is held and pooled. Every trial that was looked at and not pooled is in ONE screening log, whatever it failed on, including the four that reached this review only by reconciliation against a published review's included-study table. Each row names the criterion it fails and the quantity it reports instead -- with ONE row that does neither, and says so: a trial that could not be retrieved at all is recorded as undetermined, with what was established, the document it was established from, what could not be, and the date each attempt was made. That row is not an exclusion and is not counted as one. There is exactly ONE SOURCE list, `screening.records`. The object does also hold a second array, `screening.excluded`, and it is not a second table in any sense a reader has to reconcile: it is a view COMPUTED from the records at build time, row for row, so it cannot say anything the records do not. An earlier version of this sentence claimed there was no second array at all, which was false of the structure, and a review leg was right to read the structure rather than the sentence.

verification_basis.what_verifies_this_object: Two things, and neither is a badge this repository can emit about itself. The first is that the object is the single source of truth and the page is a pure projection of it, so a claim on the page that is not in the object cannot exist. The second is a cross-family adversarial gate: the object is read by two model families with independent file access, from different vendors, each asked to find a defect in the ACTUAL object rather than to approve it.
verification_basis.what_is_not_claimed: No internal check is described as independent verification. A script that reads this object and reports that this object is consistent has confirmed consistency and nothing else, and a badge that cannot fail is worth less than no badge, because it teaches a reader to stop looking. The validator finding no defect is reported as exactly that.
verification_basis.bar: Both families must find no defect in the object. A finding about the validator is not a finding about the object and does not block.

methodological_authority.reference: Higgins JPT, Thomas J, Chandler J, Cumpston M, Li T, Page MJ, et al (editors). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions version 6.5.1. Cochrane, 2025.
methodological_authority.version_checked_how: The publisher's versions-and-changes page settles which version is current: it lists 6.5.1 as the newest release line, with entries dated 2026 and 2025, above 6.5 dated 2024. The publisher contradicts itself and the contradiction is recorded rather than resolved in silence: the Handbook landing page and the current-version index both still print version 6.5 updated August 2024. Where they conflict this object follows the version history and the per-chapter citation lines, because those are the more specific and the more recent statements.

sections_relied_on.title: Defining types of participants: which people and populations?
sections_relied_on.used_for: The population restriction to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which is what disqualifies the preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction trials.

sections_relied_on.title: Defining which comparisons will be made
sections_relied_on.used_for: The comparator restriction to enalapril. Valsartan and ramipril are different comparisons, not variants of this one.

sections_relied_on.title: Selecting, prioritizing and grouping review outcomes
sections_relied_on.used_for: Fixing the composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization as the outcome, and the boundary rule for trials whose own primary endpoint is a different quantity.

sections_relied_on.title: Meta-analysis of time-to-event outcomes
sections_relied_on.used_for: The hazard ratio as the effect measure for time-to-event data and the generic inverse-variance method that combines log hazard ratios. This is the measure and the method used here.

sections_relied_on.title: What is heterogeneity?
sections_relied_on.used_for: The distinction between clinical and methodological diversity and statistical heterogeneity. What this pool crosses -- aetiology, blinding, endpoint rank -- is documented as diversity in the uniformity table rather than smoothed away.

sections_relied_on.title: Identifying and measuring heterogeneity
sections_relied_on.used_for: The I-squared bands, cited both for the heterogeneity statement and for the GRADE inconsistency domain, which section 14.2.2 governs but prints no bands for.

sections_relied_on.title: Incorporating heterogeneity into random-effects models
sections_relied_on.used_for: The random-effects model AND the between-study variance estimator, which the effect-measure sections do not govern. The record that estimators other than DerSimonian and Laird perform better sits in its subsection 10.10.4.4 and is why restricted maximum likelihood is the headline. Running the comparison is a sensitivity choice under 10.14, not an instruction from this section; saying otherwise credited the Handbook with advice it does not give.

sections_relied_on.title: Implementing random-effects meta-analyses
sections_relied_on.used_for: The between-study variance estimator specifically: that methods other than DerSimonian and Laird perform better, that restricted maximum likelihood is the RevMan default, and that the HKSJ adjustment can be overly wide with few studies and overly narrow when the variance estimate is zero. It also gives the I-squared RevMan computes -- from the estimated variance rather than from Cochran's Q -- which is the definitional difference this object records between its own I-squared and metafor's, and the reason neither is adopted over the other.

sections_relied_on.title: Interpretation of random-effects meta-analysis with few studies
sections_relied_on.used_for: The HKSJ interval, and ONLY that. It states that excessively wide confidence intervals are not uncommon with two or even three studies, which is why this pool reports its HKSJ interval, records that it crosses the null, and neither adopts it as the headline nor discards it. It is cited nowhere in this object for the choice of variance estimator, which it does not govern.

sections_relied_on.title: Studies (not reports) as the unit of interest
sections_relied_on.used_for: The deduplication decision in the reconciliation block. Two paywalled reviews count three STUDIES where this object counts two randomisations plus a post hoc subgroup of a trial it already pools; this section is the distinction that makes recovering that subgroup a double-count rather than a recovery.

sections_relied_on.title: Sensitivity analyses
sections_relied_on.used_for: The requirement that a pooled result be shown robust to influential decisions. The leave-one-out analysis here is not decorative: it is what shows the pooled benefit rests on one trial.

sections_relied_on.title: The GRADE approach
sections_relied_on.used_for: That Cochrane has formally adopted GRADE and that reviews should use it to evaluate certainty for important outcomes, with MECIR C74 making the five considerations mandatory and C75 making the justification of each mandatory.

sections_relied_on.title: Domains that can lead to decreasing the certainty level of a body of evidence
sections_relied_on.used_for: The five downgrade domains and the rating vocabulary. The certainty here is COMPUTED from the domains and checked against them.

cascade.primary_not_best_because: All five layers hold this cell and the two regulator layers rank higher, so the choice has to be argued rather than assumed. What this cell STORES is a point estimate WITH a two-sided 95% interval, and that interval is printed only by the primary publication. The FDA statistical review assesses the endpoint against a one-sided alpha and the EPAR prints a one-sided p value beside the point estimate; taking the point from one layer and the interval from another would manufacture a quantity no source states. The regulator layers are therefore used to CONFIRM the counts, the denominators and the point estimate, which they do exactly, and the layer that prints the stored interval is named as its source.
cascade.agreement_note: Every layer checked holds this cell and none disagrees with another. The event counts and both denominators are identical across the journal, the registry, the FDA statistical review, the EPAR and the prior synthesis. The FDA review goes further than the rest and splits the composite into cardiovascular deaths occurring as a first event plus heart failure hospitalizations occurring as a first event; those parts sum exactly to the arm total the other layers report, so the layers agree on the decomposition and not merely on the total. The percentages the EPAR prints are each arm's stored event count over its stored denominator, and the journal prints the same figures to one fewer decimal place.

source_quotes: At the time of study closure, the primary outcome had occurred in 914 patients (21.8%) in the LCZ696 group and 1117 patients (26.5%) in the enalapril group (hazard ratio in the LCZ696 group, 0.80; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.87; P<0.001).

In this double-blind trial, we randomly assigned 8442 patients with class II, III, or IV heart failure and an ejection fraction of 40% or less to receive either LCZ696 (at a dose of 200 mg twice daily) or enalapril (at a dose of 10 mg twice daily), in addition to recommended therapy.

The primary outcome was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes or hospitalization for heart failure, but the trial was designed to detect a difference in the rates of death from cardiovascular causes.

Drugs@FDA was searched for a later review naming this trial and none exists: it is a post-approval trial that supported no US labelling change. regulator_ema.reason: The Entresto EPAR and its published variation assessments predate this trial and do not contain it. The EMA medicine page was searched on the date recorded here for a later assessment naming it, and none is published.

prior_meta.reason: The prior syntheses that pool this trial are the paired Chagas reviews staged under SR_CHAGAS_PAIR, and they cannot yield this cell. Their abstracts are staged and readable and report only pooled RISK RATIOS across the whole set they include -- a different quantity from this row's time-to-first hazard ratio, and not reported per trial in any case. Their full texts, where a per-trial extraction would be, are paywalled: each returned a payment-required response when fetched on the date recorded here and neither has an open-access copy. So this layer was checked at the only depth available and holds nothing for this cell. The count discrepancy their abstracts DO create is recorded against the reconciliation block rather than here.

cascade.agreement_note: Both layers that hold this cell agree, once the difference in FORM is taken into account, which is the whole reason this note exists. The registry posts this endpoint only as a percentage of each arm; the journal posts counts. Applying each posted percentage to that arm's stored denominator reproduces the journal's count to the nearest patient, so the layers carry the same figures in two shapes. The hazard ratio itself is posted by the journal alone: the registry record attaches no analysis to this outcome. That is why the registry cannot substitute for the publication here, and saying so is the point of recording what each layer yielded rather than only that it was checked.

source_quotes: The first secondary end point was the composite of time to first HF hospitalization or death from cardiovascular causes ( Figure 2 , C, D, and E), which occurred in 155 patients (33.5%) in the sacubitril/valsartan group and 169 (36.7%) in the enalapril group (HR, 0.91 [95% CI, 0.73-1.13])

The primary end point was a hierarchical composite outcome tested, in order, of death from cardiovascular causes, hospitalization for HF, or relative change in NT-proBNP from baseline to 12 weeks. The primary analysis was done using a win ratio approach.
Overall, 462 participants were randomized to receive sacubitril/valsartan and 460 to receive enalapril (mean [SD] age, 64.2 [10.8] years; 387 [42.0%] were female).
provenance.quote_note: The first quote is the cell, and it names the endpoint as SECONDARY in the trial's own words, which is the fact that governs how this row may be used. The second is staged deliberately: this trial's PRIMARY analysis is a win ratio, a quantity that is not a hazard ratio and is never pooled here, and an object that took the row without showing that would look like it had pooled the trial's headline. The third fixes both denominators.

cvdeath_or_hfh_first.estimand_rank_note: This trial enters the pool through a SECONDARY endpoint, and that is a deliberate, stated choice rather than an oversight. The frozen question fixes the measure -- a time-to-first hazard ratio for cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization -- and this trial reports exactly that quantity, separately, with its own interval. Its PRIMARY endpoint is a hierarchical composite analysed by win ratio, which shares no scale with a hazard ratio and would answer a different question. Taking the trial's headline because it is the headline would be the error; taking the quantity the question asks for, and labelling where it sits in the trial's own hierarchy, is the alternative. discrepancies.why_it_matters: Our own multi-source extraction pass did not record this discrepancy at all. A blinded comparator found it. The two sources disagree on both numerator and denominator for the same quantity in the same trial, and we carried only one side without noticing the other existed. resolution.the_notation_defect_found_first: THE RECORDED VALUE "169/183" WAS NEVER A FRACTION. It is the two PER-ARM counts -- 169 on sacubitril/valsartan and 183 on enalapril -- written with a slash that reads as events-over-denominator. The denominators are 462 and 460, matching this trial's own arms block. Anyone reading it, including a blinded reviewer, would take it as a fraction, and the comparison against "211/234" then looks like a mismatch of BOTH numerator and denominator rather than two clean per-arm comparisons. A SLASH BETWEEN TWO SAME-KIND COUNTS IS AMBIGUOUS BY CONSTRUCTION.
resolution.the_cause_in_the_registry_own_words: "Adverse events were reported from first dose of study treatment until end of study treatment plus 30 days post treatment, up to a maximum duration of 55 months. Deaths were also collected in the survival follow-up phase from 31 days after last dose of study medication until the end of the study, for an additional 8 months. These were not considered AEs." -- ClinicalTrials.gov timeFrame, verbatim, read 2026-08-18.
resolution.what_a_reader_needs: NEITHER NUMBER IS WRONG. THEY ANSWER DIFFERENT QUESTIONS. The registry counts ON-TREATMENT serious adverse events plus a 30-day window; the publication counts the full study period. The publication figures are higher in BOTH arms (211 vs 169, 234 vs 183), which is exactly what a longer observation window produces. This is a fact about how safety data is reported, NOT a defect in either source, and it is more useful to a reader than either figure alone.
resolution.neither_value_is_adopted_over_the_other: Both stand, each labelled with its window. The original decision to record both and refuse to choose was correct; what was missing was the reason.
resolution.owed_but_optional: The JAMA supplementary appendix would state the publication window in the paper's own words and make the statement symmetric. AVAILABLE IF WANTED, NOT NEEDED -- it cannot change the answer. FDA/EMA documents were NOT retrieved and are not required: the registry carries the resolving fact in its own declaration.
resolution.found_by_an_outside_check: This discrepancy was surfaced by a BLINDED HEAD-TO-HEAD COMPARATOR on 2026-08-12, not by our own multi-source extraction pass, which did not record it at all. handbook.decision: POOL four trials reporting the same effect measure for the same outcome concept against the same comparator, producing an AVERAGE ACROSS documented differences in aetiology, ejection-fraction ceiling, blinding and the endpoint's rank within its own trial
handbook.conformance: Sections 3.2.1, 3.2.3 and 3.2.4 fix the three axes of the question -- population, comparator, outcome -- and every include and exclude decision in this object names which of the three it turns on, which is why the exclusion table has a criterion column rather than a verdict column. Section 10.9 gives the hazard ratio as the effect measure for time-to-event data and sanctions combining log hazard ratios by generic inverse variance; all four trials report a Cox hazard ratio for the time to a first event of the same composite against enalapril, so the measure is shared and not converted. What the pool crosses is documented under 10.10.1 in the uniformity table: the aetiology of the heart failure, the ejection-fraction ceiling, whether the trial was blinded, and whether this endpoint was that trial's primary or its first secondary. Not one of those is smoothed away and none is claimed to be absent. Section 10.10.4 governs the MODEL and the between-study variance estimator, which the effect-measure sections do not: it records that estimators other than DerSimonian and Laird perform better and that restricted maximum likelihood is now the default, and its subsection on few studies advises comparing the methods when there are only two or three. This pool has four, so the comparison is RUN and sits in the sensitivity block, where the three estimators do not agree closely and that is shown rather than reported as a formality. Section 10.14 is why the leave-one-out analysis is here, and in this pool it is the most important thing on the page: removing the largest trial removes the benefit.

cvdeath_or_hfh_first.poolable_reason: A single effect measure, a single comparator and a single outcome concept, across trials that share no participant and no control group.
cvdeath_or_hfh_first.estimand_id_means: the estimand of the POOLED value, which is the average this result reports. It is NOT a claim that the contributing trials estimate identical quantities. The dimensions on which they differ are listed in the uniformity table below, and the pooled value averages across them.

effect_measure: All FOUR report a hazard ratio for the time to a first event of the same composite. No conversion is performed and none would be valid: the trials excluded from this pool are excluded largely because their quantities cannot be converted into this one. This row read “all three” until 2026-08-18, when the pool had been k=4 for a day; the whole of this table described the pool as it stood before ANSWER-HF was resolved into it, which is the table that justifies the pool describing a different pool from the one published.
comparator: All four randomised against enalapril at a target of 10 mg twice daily. ANSWER-HF's own registration names enalapril as the comparator. This is the axis on which PARAGON-HF, PARAGLIDE-HF and PARADISE-MI fail, and it is checked rather than assumed.
outcome_definition: identical in the three that register it

Cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, whichever comes first. PARADIGM-HF's registered title says “First Occurrence of the Composite Endpoint, Which is Defined as Either Cardiovascular (CV) Death or Heart Failure (HF) Hospitalization”; PARALLEL-HF's registered description says “either cardiovascular (CV) death or heart failure (HF) hospitalization”; PARACHUTE-HF's registered secondary says “First Hospitalization Due to Heart Failure or Death From Cardiovascular Causes”, counted “to the first occurrence”. All three are read from the registry and quoted in full in the endpoint-definition table. ANSWER-HF REGISTERS NO SUCH ENDPOINT, so on that trial there is nothing to compare and this row does not claim there is. Its publication reports the same two components in the same first-event structure, which is agreement of the reported quantity and not of the registered one.
endpoint_registered_in_its_own_trial: THREE OF THE FOUR TRIALS REGISTERED THIS ENDPOINT BEFORE THEY RAN; ONE DID NOT. PARADIGM-HF and PARALLEL-HF register it as their primary outcome and PARACHUTE-HF as the first of six secondaries. ANSWER-HF registers neither it nor anything equivalent, at any rank, and its registration is not silent by omission -- it declares twenty outcome measures and this is not among them. A quarter of this pool therefore has no protection against selective outcome reporting, and the trial concerned is the one whose estimate is furthest from the rest. It stays in, because removing it would convert a null into a positive result, and a withdrawal needs the same evidence as a claim.
aetiology_of_heart_failure: PARACHUTE-HF and ANSWER-HF admitted only chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy, confirmed serologically at entry -- a distinct disease with a different natural history and a high burden of conduction disease. Neither PARADIGM-HF nor PARALLEL-HF restricted aetiology at all, so the pool crosses two narrow-aetiology trials with two unrestricted ones, and that is the most substantive thing it crosses. It is also HALF the pool rather than a third, which is what this row said before ANSWER-HF was counted into it. What the contributing trials' own sources say about their aetiology MIX differs in how much they say, and this row says only what they support: the EPAR records ischaemic cardiac disease as the primary cause of heart failure in the majority of PARADIGM-HF participants, and the staged sources for PARALLEL-HF characterise its population by ejection fraction and functional class without describing its aetiology mix at all. An earlier version of this row described both unrestricted trials as largely ischaemic or idiopathic; a review leg was right that the second half of that had no basis in anything staged, and it is the more serious kind of over-claim for sitting inside the table that justifies pooling across aetiology.
ejection_fraction_ceiling: 40% or less in PARADIGM-HF and PARACHUTE-HF; 35% or less in PARALLEL-HF; ANSWER-HF enrolled Chagas cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction. All are within the reduced-ejection-fraction population the question fixes, and they are not the same entry criterion.
blinding: PARADIGM-HF and PARALLEL-HF were double-blind. PARACHUTE-HF was OPEN-LABEL with blinded endpoint adjudication. Blinded adjudication protects the outcome ascertainment and does not protect the management decisions that lead to a hospitalization, so the difference is carried into the GRADE risk-of-bias domain rather than dismissed here.
endpoint_rank_within_its_own_trial: This composite is the PRIMARY endpoint of PARADIGM-HF and of PARALLEL-HF. In PARACHUTE-HF it is the first SECONDARY endpoint, the primary there being a hierarchical composite analysed by win ratio. A trial is not powered for its secondary endpoints, and the pool crosses that. IN ANSWER-HF IT HAS NO RANK, because it is not registered: that trial's registered primaries are change in ejection fraction and a four-level hierarchical win ratio. “Unregistered” is a fourth state on this axis and not a third kind of secondary.
follow_up_length: Medians of 27 months, 25.2 months and 33.9 months in the three trials that report one; ANSWER-HF's registered outcome window is 6 months, the shortest in the pool by a factor of four. PARADIGM-HF's follow-up ended early by prespecified rule when a boundary for overwhelming benefit was crossed, which is a different reason for a follow-up length than the others have. A composite counted to first event over 6 months and the same composite counted over 34 months are not the same exposure to risk, and this is the dimension on which the pool's shortest trial is also its most discrepant estimate.
analysis_population: All four use the trial's own full analysis set. In PARACHUTE-HF and ANSWER-HF that equals the randomised total; in PARADIGM-HF and PARALLEL-HF it is smaller, and each cell shows the arithmetic from the randomised total rather than leaving the difference unexplained.

heterogeneity.tau2_estimator: REML -- copied from this block's declared `estimator`, which is the authoritative record of how the pool was computed. NOT inferred: an object that declared no estimator would be left undeclared here, because the absence is itself the finding.
heterogeneity.i2_definition: REML/metafor I-squared = tau-squared / (tau-squared + typical within-study variance), where the typical variance is the Higgins-Thompson s-squared. This is what metafor's rma() reports and it is NOT (Q - df) / Q.
heterogeneity.i2_definition_evidence: Decided by recomputing BOTH definitions from this object's own per-trial inputs: REML/metafor gives 32.8940 and Higgins gives 41.8749 against the stored 32.8939. THIS OBJECT CARRIES THE MINORITY DEFINITION IN THIS CORPUS -- 10 blocks carry Higgins and this is the only decidable block carrying the other.

cvdeath_or_hfh_first.heterogeneity_status: I-squared is 32.9% under the registered REML estimator, 41.9% under DerSimonian-Laird and 55.7% under Paule-Mandel, and Q is 5.16 on 3 degrees of freedom (p=0.16). The estimator dependence is the finding: a single I-squared figure quoted without its estimator is not interpretable at this k. The prediction interval spans 0.686 to 1.107, which is the honest statement of how much the trials disagree.

sensitivity.method: leave-one-out, plus a comparison of between-study variance estimators
sensitivity.authority: Cochrane Handbook version 6.5.1, section 10.14: sensitivity analyses examine whether overall findings are robust to potentially influential decisions. Section 10.10.4.4 is what governs the estimator half: it records that methods other than DerSimonian and Laird estimate the between-study variance better and that restricted maximum likelihood is the RevMan default. An earlier version of this field credited that advice to section 10.10.4.5, which does not give it -- 10.10.4.5 is about INTERPRETATION with few studies and the method it compares is the confidence interval, not the variance estimator. The citation was attached to a decision it does not govern while the section that does govern it went uncited.
sensitivity.decision_under_test: Two decisions. First, whether the pooled benefit depends on any single trial -- and it does. Second, whether it depends on the choice of between-study variance estimator and interval method, which with four studies is not a formality.
sensitivity.leave_one_out_finding: Omitting PARADIGM-HF gives 0.9660 (0.7897 to 1.1818) with I-squared falling to 1.2%. The pooled effect is essentially PARADIGM-HF: the other three trials together sit at or above the null. Omitting ANSWER-HF returns exactly the previous 0.8392 (0.7429 to 0.9480), which is the arithmetic check that the new trial is the only thing that moved.

between_study_variance_method_comparison.why: Three between-study-variance estimators, each with Wald and HKSJ intervals. At k=3 Wald excluded the null and HKSJ did not; at k=4 both include it under every estimator, so the interval methods now agree. The point estimate moves from 0.872 to 0.904 across estimators, and I-squared from 32.9% to 55.7%.
between_study_variance_method_comparison.verdict: The estimator changes the point estimate from 0.872 to 0.904 and I-squared from 32.9% to 55.7%, and changes NOTHING about the conclusion: every estimator, under both Wald and HKSJ, gives an interval that includes no effect. At k=3 Wald and HKSJ disagreed about the null; at k=4 they agree.
between_study_variance_method_comparison.estimator_kept: REML with a Wald interval remains the registered headline. It is not chosen because it is the most favourable -- it is the least favourable of the three on I-squared and the narrowest on the interval, and every estimator reaches the same conclusion.

cross_engine.engine: metafor 5.0.1 under R 4.6.0, generic inverse variance on the same log point and log standard error this object stores
cross_engine.agreement: The summary agrees to within a ten-millionth on the ratio scale for the point and both bounds, and to a few parts in ten million on the between-study variance. Q and its degrees of freedom match exactly. This is a statement about two ENGINES agreeing on one arithmetic, and it is not a claim that the trials agree with each other: what the pooled trials differ on is in the uniformity table, and a cross-engine check has nothing to say about that.
cross_engine.i2_definitions_differ: The two engines report DIFFERENT I-squared values and neither is wrong. This object's is the Higgins statistic computed from Q and its degrees of freedom; metafor's is computed relative to the restricted-maximum-likelihood between-study variance. They are different quantities that share a name, a single engine could never reveal it, and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved by adopting the other engine's number.

grade.certainty_derivation: start high; risk_of_bias serious (-1), imprecision serious (-1); total -2 -> low. The risk_of_bias rating was re-examined against the completed RoB-2 assessment on 2026-08-12 and did not move; see domains.risk_of_bias.rob2_effect_on_this_rating.
grade.starting_point_because: every contributing study is a randomised controlled trial

risk_of_bias.basis_in_sources: Three separate features, each read from a staged source rather than assumed. PARACHUTE-HF describes itself as an 'open-label, multicenter randomized clinical trial' with blinded endpoint adjudication; blinded adjudication protects how an event is classified but not the unblinded management decisions that produce a heart failure hospitalization, which is one of the two components. In the same trial this composite is the first SECONDARY endpoint, the primary being a win ratio, so the result pooled here comes from that trial's secondary hierarchy and carries the multiplicity and selective-reporting exposure that goes with it; the separate question of the trial not being POWERED for this endpoint is random error and is carried in the imprecision domain, not here. PARADIGM-HF 'was stopped early, according to prespecified rules ... because the boundary for an overwhelming benefit with LCZ696 had been crossed', and a trial stopped early for benefit tends to overstate the effect it was stopped for -- which matters here because the leave-one-out analysis shows the pooled benefit rests on that trial. One level, not two: the trials are randomised, centrally adjudicated and large, and none of the three features is a failure of randomisation.

rob2_effect_on_this_rating.stated_explicitly_because: the protocol requires this question to be answered either way, so that a rating which survives an assessment is distinguishable from one that was never tested
rob2_effect_on_this_rating.why_it_does_not_move:
Two reasons, and the second is the load-bearing one.

First, RoB-2 confirmed the substance of the downgrade rather than removing it. Both assessors, independently and from different model families, rated PARACHUTE-HF domain 2 as SOME CONCERNS on the open-label deviations point, which is the first of the three features the rating was already built on. The second assessor also rated its domain 5 as SOME CONCERNS on the selective-reporting point, which is the second feature. The assessment agreed with the reasoning the rating rested on.

Second, and this is why 'no domain reached HIGH' does not discharge the downgrade: RoB-2 has no domain for a trial stopped early for benefit. Early stopping is not a randomization failure, a deviation, missing data, a measurement problem, or selective reporting of a result; it is a stopping-rule effect on the magnitude of the estimate, and the RoB-2 tool does not ask about it in any of its five domains. PARADIGM-HF was stopped early by prespecified rule for overwhelming benefit and the leave-one-out analysis shows the pooled benefit rests on that trial. That third feature is therefore untouched by a clean RoB-2 result, and it alone sustains a serious rating. Reading 'no domain HIGH' as grounds to remove the downgrade would be mistaking the silence of a tool for the absence of a problem.
rob2_effect_on_this_rating.counter_argument_recorded: The opposite reading is available and is recorded here rather than suppressed: under a common mapping, trials at SOME CONCERNS with none at HIGH support 'not serious', which would raise certainty from low to moderate. We do not adopt it, for the stopping-rule reason above, and because five of fifteen domain judgements are still unadjudicated -- changing a published certainty rating on the strength of a disagreement set nobody has resolved would be the wrong direction to move under uncertainty.
rob2_effect_on_this_rating.conditions_under_which_it_would_move: If the named human adjudicates the five open disagreements toward LOW, and separately judges that the early-stopping effect is adequately carried by the imprecision and leave-one-out analyses rather than here, then 'not serious' becomes defensible and certainty would rise to moderate. That is a human decision on the record, not an automatic consequence of the assessment.

inconsistency.why_not_downgraded_despite_the_spread: SUPERSEDED at k=4 and flagged for re-reading rather than rewritten. The previous text argued that the low I-squared band justified no downgrade while the spread was carried by imprecision. Both inputs changed: I-squared is now 32.9% to 55.7% depending on estimator, and the four point estimates run 0.80 to 1.83. Whether that still supports 'not serious' is a judgement to be re-argued, not a label to be re-applied, and it is left open rather than settled by the script that changed the numbers.
inconsistency.needs_rereading: This domain was rated on an I-squared of 14.9% at k=3. At k=4 it is 32.9% under REML, 41.9% under DerSimonian-Laird and 55.7% under Paule-Mandel, and the prediction interval spans 0.686 to 1.107. The rating is flagged for re-reading rather than silently carried forward or silently changed: a domain rating that survives a change in its own input should say so, and one that does not should be re-argued, not re-labelled.

indirectness.basis_in_sources: All four trials enrol the population the question names, randomise the intervention the question names against the comparator the question names, and report the outcome the question names. The Chagas aetiology of one trial makes its population narrower than the others, not indirect: it is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, entered on an ejection fraction of 40% or less and NYHA class II to IV, exactly as the other two are. Directness is judged against the review's own question, and this question is about heart failure with reduced ejection fraction rather than about any one aetiology of it.

imprecision.ois_note: The optimal information size is a condition section 14.2.2 makes part of adequate precision, and it is NOT computable from what this object holds: it needs an assumed control-arm risk and a target difference that no field here carries. It is therefore UNKNOWN rather than satisfied, and this sentence exists so that its absence cannot read as a pass. What can be said is that the pooled evidence carries a large absolute event count, so the downgrade below does not rest on sparse events.
imprecision.why: The ordinary interval excludes the null, which is 14.2.2's first condition, and on that alone this domain would not be downgraded. Two computed facts in this object contradict a reading of adequate precision. The Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman interval, which section 10.10.4.5 points to for exactly this number of studies, includes the null. And only one of the three leave-one-out fits keeps the null outside the interval, so the precision of the pooled estimate is a property of one trial rather than of the body of evidence. One level.

publication_bias.not_assessable_because: Three studies. The funnel-plot and regression methods for small-study effects are not interpretable below about ten, so no assessment is made and none is implied. What can be said without a test is recorded instead and is not treated as a substitute for one: all four trials are registered, all three posted results to their registry, and the two that are industry-sponsored report the composite in the direction of no benefit as well as of benefit, so there is no positive evidence of selective reporting of this endpoint. Rated not assessable, which downgrades nothing on its own.

grade.what_this_certainty_is_about: It is the certainty of the POOLED average across four trials, not of PARADIGM-HF. PARADIGM-HF on its own is a large double-blind trial whose result underpins a guideline recommendation; the thing rated here is the three-trial average, which inherits the open-label secondary endpoint of one trial and the fragility the leave-one-out analysis shows. Reading this rating as a verdict on sacubitril/valsartan would be a misreading, and the sentence is here because that misreading is the easy one.

egger.caution: Run for completeness. With k = 4 the test has almost no power and the Cochrane Handbook advises against interpreting it below about ten studies. Reported as a computed value, NOT as evidence about small-study effects. Recomputed at k = 4. The p value moved from 0.101 to 0.01056 when ANSWER-HF entered, and that movement is exactly what a test with almost no power does when a fourth point is added -- it is NOT a finding about small-study effects and must not be read as one.

bayes.method: grid integration, 201x201, flat prior on the pooled log effect and half-Cauchy(scale=1) on the between-study SD (Gelman 2006)

panels._provenance: Computed at BUILD time by metafor 5.0.1 under R 4.6.0 from the log point and log standard error this object stores. The page projects these stored values; opening it recomputes nothing, and no reader action can change any of them. RECOMPUTED AT k=4 on 2026-08-13: this whole block, including its own `fit`, was still the k=3 analysis after ANSWER-HF entered the pool, so a leave-one-out of three rows and a prediction interval from three trials were being shown beside a four-trial headline. peters.note: Peters 2006 regresses the log odds ratio on the inverse of total sample size, which the Cochrane Handbook v6.5 section 13.3.5 recommends for binary outcomes in place of Egger, whose test is biased on the odds-ratio scale. With k = 4 it still has almost no power and is reported as a computed value, not as evidence. Recomputed at k=4. The intercept was stored as an EMPTY LIST and rendered on the page as an empty pair of brackets where the number belongs -- the same defect as Egger's standard error, a value the extraction failed to read presented as though the field did not apply.

benford.note: First-digit screen over the 6 event counts as read. With this few integers the comparison is descriptive only -- Benford's law is a large-sample regularity and no test statistic is computed here.

count_panels._provenance: Computed at BUILD time by metafor 5.0.1 under R 4.6.0 from the per-arm 2x2 counts stored on each trial, which were READ from the sources named on each cell. No composite was reconstructed by addition and no count was derived from a percentage. These are SEPARATE ESTIMANDS from the primary pooled hazard ratio, which is unchanged, and are shown as sensitivity, never as the headline. RECOMPUTED AT k=4 on 2026-08-14. They had been marked stale at k=3 on the grounds that recomputing needed 2x2 counts that were not available; that was wrong -- ANSWER-HF's counts for this composite, 12/95 against 8/95, were already in the object. The L'Abbe panel was therefore drawing three points beside a four-trial forest. resolved_question.headline: RESOLVED 2026-08-18. The contributing ratio IS a hazard ratio. ANSWER-HF stays in the pool, k remains 4, and the displayed estimate does not change.
resolved_question.body: This page carried an open question stating that ANSWER-HF's 1.83 (0.72 to 4.67) could not be identified as a hazard ratio and that "the source does not say that it is one". THAT WAS WRONG, AND THE SOURCE SAYS IT TWICE. The JACC full text was obtained and read on 2026-08-18. Table 2, headed "Clinical Endpoints at 6 Months", has four columns: Outcomes, Sacubitril-Valsartan, Enalapril, and -- verbatim -- "Effect HR (95% CI)". The Statistical Analysis section states, verbatim: "Time-to-event secondary outcomes were also analyzed individually using Kaplan-Meier curves and estimates of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization at 6 months reported using Cox proportional hazard models, with treatment group and research site as fixed-effect factors. HRs, 95% CIs, and 2-sided P values are reported." The measure is a hazard ratio from a Cox proportional hazards model over time to first occurrence, with treatment group and research site as fixed-effect factors.
resolved_question.identity_established_first: IDENTITY BEFORE ANY NUMBER, because this is the trial the project once conflated with PARACHUTE-HF. The document read was confirmed as ANSWER-HF by REGISTRATION ID, not by label: NCT04853758 is the only registration in the document and appears twice in a registration context -- in the abstract trailer and in the Methods. PARACHUTE-HF appears eight times and every one is a citation of a DIFFERENT trial in the Discussion, carrying its own distinct win ratio of 1.52 (1.28 to 1.82). Nothing was read from this document before that check was made.
resolved_question.the_witness_that_needs_no_methods_sectio: AN ARITHMETIC WITNESS, INDEPENDENT OF ANY SENTENCE. Table 2's all-cause death row is 8/95 against 8/95, so the crude risk ratio and the crude odds ratio are both EXACTLY 1.000 -- and the published value is 1.08. NO CRUDE MEASURE CAN PRODUCE 1.08 FROM EIGHT VERSUS EIGHT. Only an estimator using time and censoring, adjusted for site, can move that comparison off unity. The same pattern holds across all four rows, every published value exceeding its own crude risk ratio: 1.27 against 1.167, 1.42 against 1.400, 1.83 against 1.500, 1.08 against 1.000. THE TWO FIGURES THIS PAGE PREVIOUSLY QUOTED ARE UNCHANGED AND ARE RESTATED HERE SO THEY DO NOT SIMPLY VANISH: from 12/95 versus 8/95 the crude risk ratio is 1.50 and the crude odds ratio is 1.57, and neither is 1.83. That was the original observation and it was CORRECT -- it was the inference drawn from it that was wrong. Departure from the crude measures is what a Cox model DOES; it is not a sign that the measure is unidentified.
resolved_question.what_was_wrong_in_what_we_published: TWO PUBLISHED CLAIMS WERE FALSE, AND BOTH WERE OURS. First: "the source does not say that it is one" -- the column header says HR and the Methods name the model. Second, and worse: "the trial states no time-to-event analysis of this composite anywhere" -- the trial states exactly that, in the sentence quoted above. The hypothesis offered alongside them, that 1.83 might be the win ratio analysed a second way, is REFUTED: the win ratio is a four-level hierarchical statistic over cardiovascular death, heart-failure hospitalisation, NT-proBNP change and LVEF change, with intervals from bootstrap resampling, reported as 1.81 (1.27 to 2.63) in the Results and 1.80 in the Abstract -- and its clinical-outcomes-only sensitivity analysis is 0.64 (0.22 to 1.66). A statistic whose clinical-only form is 0.64 is not the source of a 1.83 on the clinical composite.
resolved_question.the_answer_was_already_in_this_object: AND THE OBJECT ALREADY HELD IT. The provenance block on this very trial and this very outcome carries model_statement_quote -- the Cox sentence above, verbatim and character-identical to the publication -- and it was present in commit 935cf870a, THE COMMIT THAT CREATED THE OPEN QUESTION, and in every commit since. The object asserted "the source does not say that it is one" in its results section while holding, one level up on the same trial, the sentence in which the source says it. The finding was not blocked by a missing fact; it was blocked by two fields that were never read against each other.
resolved_question.why_it_matters: THE DIRECTION IS THE POINT. With ANSWER-HF the pool is HR 0.8715 (0.7461 to 1.0181), which crosses one. Without it, k=3 gives 0.8333 (0.7473 to 0.9292), which does not. Dropping the trial would have converted a null result into a positive one on the strength of an exclusion we made ourselves -- and it would have been WRONG, because the ratio is exactly what the pool assumed it was. A withdrawal needs the same evidentiary standard as a claim: withdrawing a correct estimate destroys a true finding and publishes the destruction as a discovery.
resolved_question.what_is_displayed: The estimate shown is the k=4 value, HR 0.8715 (0.7461 to 1.0181), and it has not changed. What has changed is this paragraph: a question is now an answer. No displayed number moved.
resolved_question.composite_definition_confirmed: The row is a FIRST-EVENT UNION despite a caption reading "and", and Table 2's own arithmetic proves it: cardiovascular death 7 and heart-failure hospitalisation 7 sum to 14 while the composite counts 12, so two patients had both and are counted once; in the control arm 6 and 5 sum to 11 against a composite of 8. The caption_trap recorded on this trial is confirmed, not assumed.
resolved_question.history: The open question was published at 935cf870a as a hand edit of the built page, existing in no object, and the first rebuild deleted it -- caught only because the new page's numerals were counted against the served page before pushing. It was moved into the object at 777a8393f. It is answered here, in the object, for the same reason: a finding that lives only in the artefact dies at the next build.
resolved_question.sensitivity_stated: SENSITIVITY, RETAINED RATHER THAN DELETED. With ANSWER-HF: HR 0.8715 (0.7461 to 1.0181), k=4 -- NULL. Without it: 0.8333 (0.7473 to 0.9292), k=3 -- NOT NULL. This is kept on the page now that the question is settled, because a reader who saw the earlier version is entitled to check the arithmetic that the resolution turns on, and because the k=4 headline being null is a fact about how much one small trial carries.

pool_uniformity_superseded_2026_08_18.why: Every row of the previous table described THREE trials while the pool published FOUR. ANSWER-HF appeared in none of the nine rows. The table that justifies the pool was describing a different pool from the one on the page. Kept here so the change can be read rather than taken on trust; no pooled number changed.

effect_measure: All three report a hazard ratio for the time to a first event of the same composite. No conversion is performed and none would be valid: the trials excluded from this pool are excluded largely because their quantities cannot be converted into this one.
comparator: All three randomised against enalapril at a target of 10 mg twice daily. This is the axis on which PARAGON-HF, PARAGLIDE-HF and PARADISE-MI fail, and it is checked rather than assumed.
outcome_definition: Cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, whichever comes first, with adjudication by a central committee in each trial.
aetiology_of_heart_failure: PARACHUTE-HF admitted only chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy, confirmed serologically at entry -- a distinct disease with a different natural history and a high burden of conduction disease. Neither of the other trials restricted aetiology at all, so the pool crosses a narrow-aetiology trial with two unrestricted ones, and that is the most substantive thing it crosses. What the contributing trials' own sources say about their aetiology MIX differs in how much they say, and this row says only what they support: the EPAR records ischaemic cardiac disease as the primary cause of heart failure in the majority of PARADIGM-HF participants, and the staged sources for PARALLEL-HF characterise its population by ejection fraction and functional class without describing its aetiology mix at all. An earlier version of this row described both unrestricted trials as largely ischaemic or idiopathic; a review leg was right that the second half of that had no basis in anything staged, and it is the more serious kind of over-claim for sitting inside the table that justifies pooling across aetiology.
ejection_fraction_ceiling: 40% or less in PARADIGM-HF and PARACHUTE-HF; 35% or less in PARALLEL-HF. Both are within the reduced-ejection-fraction population the question fixes, and they are not the same entry criterion.
blinding: PARADIGM-HF and PARALLEL-HF were double-blind. PARACHUTE-HF was OPEN-LABEL with blinded endpoint adjudication. Blinded adjudication protects the outcome ascertainment and does not protect the management decisions that lead to a hospitalization, so the difference is carried into the GRADE risk-of-bias domain rather than dismissed here.
endpoint_rank_within_its_own_trial: This composite is the PRIMARY endpoint of PARADIGM-HF and of PARALLEL-HF. In PARACHUTE-HF it is the first SECONDARY endpoint, the primary there being a hierarchical composite analysed by win ratio. A trial is not powered for its secondary endpoints, and the pool crosses that.
follow_up_length: Medians of 27 months, 25.2 months and 33.9 months. PARADIGM-HF's follow-up ended early by prespecified rule when a boundary for overwhelming benefit was crossed, which is a different reason for a follow-up length than the other two have.
analysis_population: All three use the trial's own full analysis set. In PARACHUTE-HF that equals the randomised total; in PARADIGM-HF and PARALLEL-HF it is smaller, and each cell shows the arithmetic from the randomised total rather than leaving the difference unexplained.

eligibility_of_an_unregistered_endpoint.question: ANSWER-HF (NCT04853758) registers this endpoint at NO rank. Should a trial whose contributed endpoint is absent from its own registration be ELIGIBLE to contribute to the pool at all?
eligibility_of_an_unregistered_endpoint.decision: IT STAYS IN THE PRIMARY ANALYSIS. The absence is graded as RISK OF BIAS, not as ineligibility, and k=3 is reported as a sensitivity analysis.
eligibility_of_an_unregistered_endpoint.authority: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, Version 6.5 (2024), section 8.7 -- RoB 2 domain 5, 'bias in selection of the reported result'. That domain covers bias arising when 'the reported result is selected (based on its direction, magnitude or statistical significance) from among multiple intervention effect estimates that were calculated by the trial authors', and its stated method is to 'attempt to retrieve the pre-specified analysis intentions for each trial ... allows for the identification of any outcome measures or analyses that have been omitted from, or added to, the results report, post hoc'. AN ENDPOINT ADDED POST HOC IS WHAT SECTION 8.7 EXISTS TO GRADE. Eligibility is Chapter 3's business -- participants, interventions, comparators, outcomes and study design -- and registration status is not among its criteria. Nothing in the Handbook makes an unregistered analysis ineligible.
eligibility_of_an_unregistered_endpoint.sensitivity_authority: Section 10.14: 'Sensitivity analyses should be used to examine whether overall findings are robust to potentially influential decisions.'
eligibility_of_an_unregistered_endpoint.handbook_version_verified: Version 6.5, 2024, read live on 2026-08-18 at https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current . NOTE: this object's `sensitivity.authority` field says '6.5.1'; the current Handbook page states '6.5'. Recorded as verified rather than reconciled, because a remembered point-release number is exactly the kind of citation this check exists to stop.
eligibility_of_an_unregistered_endpoint.why_this_ordering_and_not_the_reverse: Excluding the trial converts a null result into a positive one BY OUR OWN CHOICE, and the Handbook gives no basis for the exclusion. Presenting the exclusion as a sensitivity analysis discloses the same fact without letting our judgement manufacture the finding. The DIRECTION of the error decides: a wrong inclusion leaves a null intact; a wrong exclusion publishes a positive result we created.
eligibility_of_an_unregistered_endpoint.rob2_consequence: RoB 2 domain 5 is graded HIGH RISK for ANSWER-HF on this result, with the registry enumeration as the evidence: twenty outcome measures declared, two primary and eighteen secondary, none a first-event union of cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisation.

sensitivity_result.interpretation: Excluding ANSWER-HF gives 0.8333 (0.7473-0.9292), which does not cross one, against the primary 0.8715 (0.7461-1.0181), which does. THIS IS REPORTED AS A SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS AND IS NOT THE PAGE'S ESTIMATE. It is stated in full precisely because the direction is uncomfortable: a reader is entitled to know that the null depends on the trial with the weakest pre-specification.

eligibility_of_an_unregistered_endpoint.what_this_does_not_establish: NOT that ANSWER-HF's estimate is wrong -- the measure question was separately resolved and 1.83 (0.72-4.67) is a hazard ratio. NOT that the pool is correct: the other uniformity axes (aetiology, follow-up length, ejection-fraction ceiling) differ and are stated separately on the page. This field decides ELIGIBILITY only.

unregistered_endpoint_handbook_ruling.what_the_registry_declares: TWENTY outcome measures -- two primary, eighteen secondary, none 'other' -- and not one is a first-event union of cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisation. Its only measure naming both components is a four-level hierarchical WIN RATIO, a different estimand.
unregistered_endpoint_handbook_ruling.consequence: EXCLUDING THIS TRIAL WOULD MOVE THE RESULT FROM NULL TO POSITIVE: k=4 gives HR 0.8715 (0.7461-1.0181), which crosses one; k=3 gives 0.8333 (0.7473-0.9292), which does not. WE DID NOT EXCLUDE IT. The k=3 value is reported as a sensitivity analysis and is stated in full precisely because its direction is uncomfortable: a reader is entitled to know that the null depends on the trial with the weakest pre-specification.
unregistered_endpoint_handbook_ruling.ruled_by: Mahmood, 2026-08-18: keep ANSWER-HF in the main analysis and mark it high risk -- and 'use handbook to decide for me'. The Handbook was therefore checked for the two findings that would OVERTURN that ruling before it was applied. Both fail. See how_this_was_verified.

authority.question: A contributing trial's registration does not declare the endpoint this synthesis takes from it. Is that an ELIGIBILITY question or a RISK OF BIAS question, and must the result be excluded from the primary synthesis?
authority.answer: RISK OF BIAS, not eligibility. The result STAYS in the primary synthesis, the trial is graded at high risk of bias in the domain covering selection of the reported result, and any analysis excluding it is reported as a SENSITIVITY analysis.

it_is_a_risk_of_bias_question.what: RoB 2 domain 5, 'bias in selection of the reported result'.
it_is_a_risk_of_bias_question.verbatim_scope: Covers bias arising when 'the reported result is selected (based on its direction, magnitude or statistical significance) from among multiple intervention effect estimates that were calculated by the trial authors'.
it_is_a_risk_of_bias_question.verbatim_method: 'attempt to retrieve the pre-specified analysis intentions for each trial ... allows for the identification of any outcome measures or analyses that have been omitted from, or added to, the results report, post hoc'.
it_is_a_risk_of_bias_question.why_it_fits: An outcome ADDED post hoc is precisely what this domain exists to grade. Our three instances are all of that kind -- the quantity exists in the publication and not in the registration.

it_is_NOT_an_eligibility_question.verbatim_3_1: 'Outcomes usually are not part of the criteria for including studies, and a Cochrane review would typically seek all sufficiently rigorous studies (most commonly randomized trials) of a particular comparison of interventions in a particular population of participants, irrespective of the outcomes measured or reported.'
it_is_NOT_an_eligibility_question.verbatim_3_2_4_1: 'Reporting of outcomes should rarely determine study eligibility for a review. In particular, studies should not be excluded because they do not report results of an outcome they may have measured, or provide "no usable data".'
it_is_NOT_an_eligibility_question.verbatim_mecir_3_2_d: 'Outcome measures should not always form part of the criteria for including studies in a review.'
it_is_NOT_an_eligibility_question.so: The Handbook does not merely permit inclusion -- it DISCOURAGES using outcome reporting as an eligibility criterion at all. Eligibility rests on the PICO elements and study design. Registration status is not among them.

the_handbook_does_not_require_exclusion.chapter: 13 (bias due to missing results in a synthesis)
the_handbook_does_not_require_exclusion.finding: Chapter 13 nowhere recommends excluding a non-pre-specified result from the primary synthesis. Its recommended handling is DETECTION (13.3.1.3, comparing study plans against available results), a RISK OF BIAS JUDGEMENT using the ROB-ME tool (13.3.5), and SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS (13.3.4.6) -- not exclusion.
the_handbook_does_not_require_exclusion.and_a_distinction_that_matters: Chapter 13 and ROB-ME address results MISSING from a synthesis. Our case is the opposite direction -- a result PRESENT that was never pre-specified -- which is why section 8.7 is the correct instrument and Chapter 13 is the adjacent one. Section 8.7 says so itself: it 'does not address bias due to selective non-reporting (or incomplete reporting) of outcome domains that were measured and analysed by the trial authors'.

sensitivity_analysis_authority.verbatim: 'Sensitivity analyses should be used to examine whether overall findings are robust to potentially influential decisions.'

authority.the_conservative_principle: WHERE THE HANDBOOK LEAVES A CHOICE, TAKE THE OPTION THAT DOES NOT MOVE A RESULT TOWARD SIGNIFICANCE BY OUR OWN DECISION. An analytic choice of ours that STRENGTHENS our own conclusion needs a stronger justification than one that weakens it. Here the direction decides on its own: a wrong inclusion leaves a null intact, while a wrong exclusion publishes a positive result we created.
authority.how_this_was_verified: The ruling to adopt this reading came from the author. An author's agreement is not a source, so both propositions that would OVERTURN it were tested before it was applied: (1) does the Handbook place a non-pre-specified outcome under ELIGIBILITY? Chapter 3 says the opposite and discourages outcome-based exclusion. (2) is it explicit that such results should be EXCLUDED from primary synthesis? Chapter 13 recommends detection, a risk-of-bias judgement and sensitivity analysis instead. Both fail; the Handbook is more emphatic than the ruling.

step_2_pooled_estimate.reading: Agreement to six decimal places. The residual is rounding in the stored log inputs, not a difference in method. REML random-effects, k=4.

step_3_heterogeneity_AND_A_LABELLING_DEF.i2_DISCREPANCY_RESOLVED: I-squared did NOT match on first comparison: 41.87 recomputed against 32.89 on the object, a 9-point gap that is not rounding. IT IS A DIFFERENCE OF DEFINITION, and both are correct. Higgins I-squared = (Q - df)/Q = 41.8749. The metafor/REML formulation, I-squared = tau-squared / (tau-squared + typical within-study variance), gives 32.8940 against the object's 32.8939087126 -- agreement to four decimal places. THE OBJECT'S VALUE IS RIGHT AND ITS LABEL IS INCOMPLETE: the field is named 'i2' and does not say which definition it reports. A reader comparing it to a Higgins I-squared computed from the same Q would conclude the object was wrong.

records.reason: This is the hardest exclusion in the table and the only one that passes the population and the comparator: 190 patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction due to Chagas cardiomyopathy, randomised double-blind against ENALAPRIL. It fails on the MEASURE. Its primary endpoint is the change in left-ventricular ejection fraction at six months, and its only composite analysis of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization is inside a hierarchical endpoint analysed by WIN RATIO, reported as 1.80 with a 95% interval of 1.27 to 2.63. records.the_rule_this_applies: A trial with the right population and the right comparator enters this pool only if it separately reports the quantity the question fixes. A win ratio is not a hazard ratio: it is a count of pairwise wins over an ordered hierarchy, it has no interpretation as a ratio of hazards, and pooling it with hazard ratios would average two different questions. Six months of follow-up in 190 patients would also contribute very few events. The trial is shown here, with its quantity, rather than deleted -- if a hazard ratio for this composite is published later, this entry is where the recovery starts.

evidence_basis.why_this_is_not_our_estimand: Our frozen estimand is the time to a FIRST event of cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure. A randomised comparison of sacubitril/valsartan with enalapril, 52 against 45, in pulmonary hypertension due to heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, followed for six months. dual_screening.systematic_pattern: All 91 disagreements are screener B answering UNDETERMINED where screener A answered EXCLUDE. Not one is a straight include/exclude conflict. Two of them are PARACHUTE-HF and ANSWER-HF -- the two trials later adjudicated INTO the review by the named human. A second screener would have flagged both for adjudication before the fact rather than after.
dual_screening.limitation_of_this_instrument: The prompt given to screener B said that an undetermined later resolved is worth more than a confident wrong exclusion. That wording plausibly pushed it toward undetermined, and 91 of 91 disagreements running one way is consistent with an induced bias as well as with genuine caution. The agreement rate is therefore reported as measured but should NOT be read as an unbiased estimate of inter-screener reliability. Re-running screener B on neutral wording is the check, and it has not been done.

trial_list_diffs.review_scope: sacubitril/valsartan against enalapril in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction due to Chagas cardiomyopathy
trial_list_diffs.access_limitation: Both reviews are staged, at the depth that is open. Their ABSTRACTS are readable and are in the bundle, and they are the source of the patient total below. Their FULL TEXTS are paywalled -- each returned a payment-required response when fetched on the date recorded here, and neither has a PubMed Central or other open-access copy -- and the full text is where the included-study LIST lives. The count is therefore checkable and the list is not, which is the whole shape of this unresolved item.
trial_list_diffs.count_discrepancy: RESOLVED, and the resolution reverses what an earlier version of this object concluded. Both reviews report a pooled total of 1225 patients, 615 against 610, across a study count larger than the Chagas TRIALS this object can identify. The earlier text treated the shortfall as an entire randomised trial that the search had missed. It is not a trial. The staged ANSWER-HF registry record states in its own background that a post hoc analysis of PARADIGM-HF in chagasic cardiomyopathy, by Ramires and colleagues, reported on 113 patients treated with sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril -- and adding that subgroup to the two Chagas trials reproduces the reviews' total exactly.
trial_list_diffs.why_it_is_not_recovered: Because recovering it would be a unit-of-analysis error, not a gain. A post hoc Chagas subgroup of PARADIGM-HF is not a separate randomisation: those patients are already inside the PARADIGM-HF row this object pools, and entering them again as a third cohort would count the same randomised participants and the same control group twice. The reviews' count of studies is a count of REPORTS; this object's k is a count of RANDOMISATIONS, and the two are not the same quantity. That is the same distinction the Handbook draws in section 4.6.1 between studies and reports, applied in the direction that costs a study rather than the direction that adds one.
trial_list_diffs.what_this_says_about_the_reviews: Nothing critical, and this object is not in a position to be critical: their full texts are paywalled, so how they handled the overlap cannot be read. Pooling a subgroup of PARADIGM-HF alongside two independent Chagas trials would be a unit-of-analysis problem only if PARADIGM-HF itself were also in their pool, and it is not -- their question is Chagas-only. The observation is recorded because it explains their count, not because it impeaches it.
trial_list_diffs.disposition: resolved by a staged source, and recorded as a deduplication decision
trial_list_diffs.why_it_does_not_change_the_pool: It does not change k and it must not. The patients it names are PARADIGM-HF patients, already counted once in this pool at the level of the randomisation they belong to. An earlier version of this field said the opposite -- that nothing about the shortfall was known, not even a name -- and that had stopped being true the moment the ANSWER-HF registry record was staged. A stated unknown is something a reader trusts, so carrying one that the bundle itself refutes is worse than the gap it was describing.

reconciliation.access_limitation: One comparison review was fully readable and its included-study table is what made this reconciliation possible. The other relevant reviews -- those covering the Chagas sub-question -- are paywalled: each returned a payment-required response when fetched on the date recorded here and none has an open-access copy, so their included-study LISTS could not be read and only their abstracts could. Where a list could not be read, no agreement is claimed from a matching count: that is the coincidence-of-counts overclaim this step exists to avoid, and the arithmetic that fails to reconcile is written out instead.

SCOPE:measure-is-part-of-the-question.decision: Only a time-to-first-event hazard ratio for the composite enters the pool. Recurrent-event rate ratios, hierarchical win ratios and biomarker ratios-of-change do not, whatever the trial calls them.
SCOPE:measure-is-part-of-the-question.conformance: Section 3.2.4 makes the outcome a defining criterion of the review rather than a reporting preference, and section 10.9 fixes the hazard ratio as the measure for time-to-event data and the generic inverse-variance method as the way to combine log hazard ratios. Together they make the measure part of the question. This is the decision that produces most of the exclusion table, and it is applied symmetrically: it excludes PARAGON-HF's rate ratio of 0.87, which is the number most likely to be mistaken for a hazard ratio because it is a plausible one, and it excludes ANSWER-HF even though ANSWER-HF has the right population and the right comparator. A criterion that bends for a trial one wants is not a criterion.
SCOPE:measure-is-part-of-the-question.SUPERSEDED_2026_08_18: SUPERSEDED 2026-08-18. THIS RECORDS A DECISION THAT WAS REVERSED. ANSWER-HF IS IN THE POOL, k=4. The measure question was resolved against the source: JACC Table 2 is headed 'Effect HR (95% CI)' and the Methods name Cox proportional hazard models, so the 1.83 (0.72-4.67) IS a hazard ratio and the exclusion ground fell away. Kept rather than deleted because a record showing a decision being corrected is worth more than one that was always right. FOUND BY AN INDEPENDENT BLINDED REVIEW, not by us.

SCOPE:secondary-endpoints-are-eligible-w.decision: A trial may contribute a SECONDARY endpoint if that endpoint is the quantity the frozen question names and is separately reported with its own interval. The rank is recorded on the row and carried into GRADE.
SCOPE:secondary-endpoints-are-eligible-w.conformance: Section 3.2.4 defines eligibility by the outcome the review is about, not by the outcome the trial chose to power. Excluding a separately reported, centrally adjudicated hazard ratio because the trial ranked something else first would make the review's scope depend on other people's design choices. The cost is real and is not hidden: a secondary endpoint carries no power guarantee and, in PARACHUTE-HF's case, sits beneath a primary that was itself positive on a different scale. That cost is real and it falls in TWO different GRADE domains, which an earlier version of this decision ran together. The part that is about SYSTEMATIC error -- that a result taken from a trial's secondary hierarchy carries multiplicity and selective-reporting exposure the primary does not -- is carried in the risk-of-bias domain, and is one of the reasons that domain is rated serious. The part that is about RANDOM error -- that the trial was not powered for this endpoint -- is not risk of bias at all and is carried in the imprecision domain, where the leave-one-out fits and the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman interval already do the work. A review leg was right that attributing a power argument to risk of bias confuses the two.

SCREENING:must-match-the-question-it-ser.decision: The screening rule looks for the population, the comparator and the measure this question names. It does NOT require a placebo-controlled design or a publication date after 2015.
SCREENING:must-match-the-question-it-ser.conformance: Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.3 define participants and comparisons, and a screening rule is only as good as its agreement with them. A rule requiring a placebo arm would structurally miss every trial this question is about, since the question names an active comparator; a rule excluding pre-2015 publications would drop the trial that carries most of the weight. Both rules appeared in the material this object was built from and neither survives contact with the question, which is recorded in the corrected-claims table rather than fixed in silence.
